hero.title: The History of Morocco: From Amazigh Origins to Imperial Dynasties
hero.subtitle: Explore more than two millennia of civilization at the crossroads of Africa, Europe and the Arab-Muslim world. From ancient Berber kingdoms to the architectural masterpieces of ruling dynasties.

intro.title: A Unique Crossroads of Civilizations in Africa
intro.text: Morocco's history stands out for remarkable state continuity and cultural independence in North Africa. Shielded by the high natural barriers of the Atlas and bordered by two seafronts (Atlantic and Mediterranean), the country forged a plural identity where Amazigh (Berber) heritage, Arab-Islamic influence, Andalusian currents and Saharan contacts intertwine.
intro.text2: Unlike its neighbours, Morocco was never under Ottoman rule, thus preserving its own ruling dynasties and unique architectural and craft traditions.

antiquite.title: 1. Berber Origins, Phoenician Trading Posts and Mauretania Tingitana
antiquite.p1: The first recorded inhabitants of Morocco are the Amazigh ("free people"). From the 8th century BC, Phoenician and later Carthaginian merchants established coastal trading posts (Lixus, Tingis/Tangier, Mogador/Essaouira).
antiquite.p2: The indigenous kingdom of Mauretania flourished under the learned King Juba II and his son Ptolemy. Annexed by Rome under Emperor Caligula, the province became Mauretania Tingitana. The city of Volubilis then rose as the Roman administrative capital, famed for its olive-oil presses and magnificent mosaics.

idrissides.title: 2. The Idrisid Dynasty and the Birth of the First Moroccan State
idrissides.p1: In 789, Idris I, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad fleeing the Abbasid caliphate of Baghdad, was welcomed by the Berber Awerba tribe at Walili (Volubilis). He founded the first unified Muslim Moroccan state.
idrissides.p2: His son, Idris II, made Fez the capital. In 859, under their patronage, Fatima al-Fihriya founded the Al Quaraouiyine mosque and university, recognized by UNESCO and Guinness as the oldest continuously operating university in the world. Fez then became the spiritual, cultural and intellectual beacon of North Africa.

almoravides.title: 3. The Almoravid Empire: Founders of Marrakech and Unifiers of Al-Andalus
almoravides.p1: From the nomadic Sanhaja Berber tribes of the Sahara, the Almoravids (Al-Murabitun) swept north. In 1070 their great ruler Yusuf ibn Tashfin founded Marrakech, capital of an empire stretching from the Senegal River to Muslim Spain (Al-Andalus).
almoravides.p2: After the victory of Zallaqa (1086), Yusuf ibn Tashfin incorporated the Andalusian taifa kingdoms. The Almoravids brought Andalusian architectural refinement, red pisé ramparts and sophisticated underground irrigation (khettaras) to Morocco.

almohades.title: 4. The Almohad Empire: The Peak of Monumental Architecture
almohades.p1: Born of the religious reform preached by Ibn Tumart in the High Atlas (Tinmel), the Almohads (Al-Muwahhidun) overthrew the Almoravids. Under Abd al-Mu'min and Yaqub al-Mansur, the empire reached its greatest territorial extent, uniting the whole Maghreb and Al-Andalus.
almohades.p2: The Almohads raised emblematic twin minarets: the Koutoubia in Marrakech, the Hassan Tower in Rabat and the Giralda in Seville. Rabat was given monumental walls and the majestic gate of the Kasbah of the Udayas.

merinides.title: 5. The Marinids: The Golden Age of Madrasas and Zaouia Art
merinides.p1: From the Zenata nomads, the Marinids established their capital in Fez and built Fes el-Jdid (the new imperial city) beside the old medina.
merinides.p2: Marinid sultans strongly supported education and the arts. They built the most refined Quranic schools (madrasas) of the Islamic world: Bou Inania and el-Attarine in Fez, carved in stucco, cedar and zellige. Under the Marinids, the famous Fez explorer Ibn Battuta completed his pilgrimage and 120,000 km journey across Afro-Eurasia.

saadiens.title: 6. The Saadian Dynasty: The Battle of the Three Kings and El Badi Palace
saadiens.p1: From the Draa Valley in the south, the Sharifian Saadian dynasty rose by repelling Portuguese raids on the Atlantic coast. On 4 August 1578, at the famous Battle of the Three Kings (Wadi al-Makhazin), Sultan Abdelmalek routed the army of King Sebastian I of Portugal.
saadiens.p2: Sultan Ahmed al-Mansur al-Dhahabi ("the Golden") ushered in great prosperity through the sugar trade and the Timbuktu expedition. He built the sumptuous El Badi Palace and the sublime Saadian Tombs in Iraqi marble and carved stucco in Marrakech.

alaouites.title: 7. The Alaouite Dynasty: From Moulay Ismail to the Modern Kingdom
alaouites.p1: From the Tafilalet (Rissani), the Alaouite dynasty has ruled Morocco since the 17th century. Sultan Moulay Ismail (1672–1727), a contemporary of Louis XIV, made Meknes his imperial capital, with vast walls, granaries (Heri es-Souani) and the monumental Bab Mansour gate.
alaouites.p2: After the Franco-Spanish Protectorate (1912–1956), King Mohammed V led the country to Independence. His son Hassan II consolidated territorial unity and built the great mosque of Casablanca. Today, under HM King Mohammed VI, Morocco combines infrastructure modernization (Al Boraq high-speed rail, Noor solar complex, global ports) with rigorous preservation of its craft and architectural heritage.

faq.title: FAQ on the History of Morocco
faq.q1: What are the 4 Imperial Cities of Morocco?
faq.a1: The four imperial cities chosen as capitals by successive ruling dynasties are Fez (Idrisids, Marinids), Marrakech (Almoravids, Almohads, Saadians), Meknes (Alaouites under Moulay Ismail) and Rabat (Almohads and current capital under the Alaouites).
faq.q2: Was Morocco part of the Ottoman Empire?
faq.a2: No. Morocco is the only North African country to have kept its independence from the Ottoman Empire. The Saadian then Alaouite dynasties stopped Ottoman advances at the Moulouya border (near Oujda).
faq.q3: What is the oldest continuously operating university in the world?
faq.a3: It is Al Quaraouiyine University in the Fez medina, founded in 859 by Fatima al-Fihriya.
